source_evidence.anchor: Let X₁, …, X_N be independent sub-gaussian random variables with zero means and unit variances
source_evidence.observation: The exercise concerns a nonempty numbered finite family X₁, …, X_N; every member is a real sub-gaussian random variable, the family is independent, and each member has mean zero and variance one.

source_evidence.anchor: a = (a₁, …, a_N) ∈ ℝ^N; for every p ∈ [2, ∞)
source_evidence.observation: The coefficient vector is arbitrary in ℝ^N, and the asserted two-sided estimate is required for every real p with 2 ≤ p < ∞.

source_evidence.location: PDF page 19; printed page 30, displayed inequality in Exercise 2.6.5
source_evidence.observation: The conclusion contains both directions: the Euclidean norm of a is a lower bound for the L^p norm of the sum, while C K √p times that Euclidean norm is an upper bound. Both sums run from i = 1 through N.

source_evidence.location: PDF page 19; printed page 30, final line of Exercise 2.6.5
source_evidence.anchor: where K = max_i ‖X_i‖_{ψ₂} and C is an absolute constant
source_evidence.observation: K is the maximum ψ₂ norm over the numbered family (1 ≤ i ≤ N), and the multiplicative constant C is absolute, hence independent of N, the variables, a, and p.

source_evidence.location: PDF page 16; printed page 27, Equation (2.15) and its introductory sentence
source_evidence.anchor: every sub-gaussian random variable X satisfies … ‖X‖_{L^p} ≤ C ‖X‖_{ψ₂} √p for all p ≥ 1
source_evidence.observation: The inherited moment estimate applies to every sub-gaussian random variable and every real p ≥ 1. It supplies the ψ₂-to-L^p upper bound used in the exercise's Khintchine estimate.

source_evidence.location: PDF page 16; printed page 27, paragraph following Equations (2.14)–(2.16)
source_evidence.anchor: Here C, c > 0 are absolute constants. Moreover, up to absolute constant factors, ‖X‖_{ψ₂} is the smallest possible number that makes each of these inequalities valid.
source_evidence.observation: Equation (2.15) is a characterization up to absolute multiplicative constants; its C is positive and absolute rather than dependent on X or p.

source_evidence.location: PDF page 16; printed page 27, Definition 2.5.6 and Equation (2.13)
source_evidence.observation: The ψ₂ norm occurring in K is defined as the least positive scale (expressed as the displayed infimum) at which the exponential-square moment is at most 2; a variable satisfying the equivalent conditions of Proposition 2.5.2 is called sub-gaussian.

binders: N is a positive integer; the notation X₁, …, X_N and the ranges i = 1, …, N specify a nonempty finite numbered family.
X₁, …, X_N are real random variables on a common probability space.
a = (a₁, …, a_N) is an arbitrary vector in ℝ^N.
p is arbitrary in [2, ∞), i.e. p is real and 2 ≤ p < ∞.
There is a positive absolute constant C for the upper estimate, uniform in N, the distributions of the X_i, a, and p.
hypotheses: The random variables X₁, …, X_N are mutually independent.
For every i with 1 ≤ i ≤ N, E[X_i] = 0.
For every i with 1 ≤ i ≤ N, Var(X_i) = 1. Together with the zero-mean hypothesis this gives E[X_i²] = 1.
The exercise's moment exponent satisfies p ∈ [2, ∞).
conclusions: Upper inequality: ‖Σ_{i=1}^N a_i X_i‖_{L^p} ≤ C K √p (Σ_{i=1}^N a_i²)^(1/2), where C is absolute and K = max_{1≤i≤N} ‖X_i‖_{ψ₂}.
definitions_and_conventions: The sub-gaussian norm is ‖Y‖_{ψ₂} := inf {t > 0 : E exp(Y²/t²) ≤ 2} (Definition 2.5.6, Equation (2.13)).
An absolute constant is independent of the dimension/family size, the variables and their laws, the coefficient vector, and the exponent p; its numerical value is not specified.
implicit_context: Equation (2.15) states that every sub-gaussian Y satisfies ‖Y‖_{L^q} ≤ C₀ ‖Y‖_{ψ₂} √q for every q ≥ 1, with C₀ > 0 absolute.

The paragraph following Equation (2.16) says that, up to absolute constant factors, ‖Y‖_{ψ₂} is the smallest scale making each displayed sub-gaussian characterization, including Equation (2.15), valid.
The maximum in the definition of K and every displayed sum are over precisely the same index set {1, …, N}.
Because p ≥ 2 and the X_i are independent, centered, and have unit variance, the lower bound is normalized with coefficient exactly one rather than another unspecified constant.

details: For every positive family size N, every family satisfying the stated probabilistic hypotheses, every a ∈ ℝ^N, and every p ∈ [2, ∞), the two inequalities hold with one universal absolute constant C.
K is determined by the chosen family and is not an additional freely chosen parameter.
Independence, zero means, and unit variances are all simultaneous hypotheses and apply to each numbered variable.
Unit variance plus zero mean identifies the L² norm of Σ a_i X_i with (Σ a_i²)^(1/2), which accounts for the exact lower endpoint of the two-sided estimate.
The exercise itself is restricted to p ≥ 2 and finite p.
The inherited Equation (2.15) is broader in its exponent domain: it holds for all p ≥ 1 for any sub-gaussian random variable.
The lower inequality has neither K nor √p and has constant one.
The upper inequality contains both the maximal sub-gaussian norm K and the √p growth factor, multiplied by an absolute constant.

undebatable_constraints: The family is the nonempty numbered family X₁, …, X_N, with indices 1 through N.
All X_i are independent, sub-gaussian, mean zero, and variance one.
The coefficients form an arbitrary vector a ∈ ℝ^N.
The exercise quantifies over every finite real p with p ≥ 2.
The lower bound (Σ a_i²)^(1/2) ≤ ‖Σ a_i X_i‖_{L^p} is part of the claim.
The upper bound ‖Σ a_i X_i‖_{L^p} ≤ C K √p (Σ a_i²)^(1/2) is part of the claim.
K is max_{1≤i≤N} ‖X_i‖_{ψ₂}; it cannot be replaced by an average, sum, or unrelated bound.
C is a positive absolute constant, not a parameter depending on N, i, X_i, a, p, or K.
Equation (2.15) supplies the inherited characterization ‖Y‖_{L^p} ≤ C ‖Y‖_{ψ₂} √p for all sub-gaussian Y and all p ≥ 1.

contract_plain_english: For every positive integer N, take independent real sub-gaussian random variables X₁, …, X_N, each with mean zero and variance one, and any coefficient vector a ∈ ℝ^N. With K equal to the largest ψ₂ norm among the X_i, there is a universal positive constant C such that for every finite p ≥ 2, the L^p norm of Σ_{i=1}^N a_i X_i lies between ‖a‖₂ and C K √p ‖a‖₂, inclusive. The inherited Equation (2.15) says more generally that every sub-gaussian Y obeys ‖Y‖_{L^p} ≤ C₀ ‖Y‖_{ψ₂} √p for every p ≥ 1, where C₀ is absolute and the ψ₂ norm is, up to absolute factors, the least scale for such characterizations.
